title: Further Reading
html:
These references extend the engineering decisions discussed throughout the book. The primary documentation is useful when implementing a particular mechanism or checking a provider’s guarantees. The books and research accounts offer more detailed treatments of the underlying ideas.

Documentation changes as software evolves. When applying an example, check the version, configuration, and API your application actually uses. A newer release may provide guarantees or behavior that your deployed version does not support.

Primary Documentation

Deadlines and cancellation: Chapters 4 and 14.

The gRPC guide explains deadline handling, cancellation, and passing the available time between services. Language-specific support and application cleanup still require verification.

https://grpc.io/docs/guides/deadlines/

HTTP/2 streams: Chapter 4.

RFC 9113 specifies HTTP/2, including streams, multiplexing, and flow control. It provides background for distinguishing concurrent requests from physical connections. TCP packet loss can delay delivery across streams sharing a connection.

https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html

Provider idempotency: Chapters 3 and 14.

Stripe’s documentation provides a concrete example of an idempotency contract, including parameter comparison and result retention. Its guarantees apply to the documented API. Other providers, endpoints, and API versions require their own integration review.

https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests

Replication and commit durability: Chapters 7 and 14.

The PostgreSQL documentation explains standby replication and the acknowledgment behavior controlled by synchronous_commit. These references are useful when separating receipt, durable storage, replay, and read visibility.

https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/warm-standby.html

https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html

Table partitioning: Chapter 7.

PostgreSQL describes partition bounds, pruning, and constraints, including restrictions on uniqueness across a partitioned table.

https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-partitioning.html

Data extraction and tenant isolation: Chapter 11.

PostgreSQL documents logical replication and row-level security. The former is relevant to transferring data authority during service extraction. The latter specifies which roles and operations are subject to row policies, including important bypass behavior.

https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logical-replication.html

https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-rowsecurity.html

Service objectives and alerting: Chapter 8.

“Alerting on SLOs” in The Site Reliability Workbook develops error-budget burn rates and multi-window alerting. The examples help explain why alert windows and traffic volume need to be considered together.

https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/

Telemetry and collector pipelines: Chapter 8.

OpenTelemetry documents metrics, traces, and logs, the OTLP protocol, and Collector pipelines. The Collector reference is useful for understanding receivers, processors, and exporters. Backend compatibility also depends on supported attributes and semantic conventions.

https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/signals/

https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otlp/

https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/configuration/

Container lifecycle and deployment: Chapters 6 and 10.

The Kubernetes documentation describes startup, readiness, and liveness probes, along with Deployment rollout behavior. These are the implementation references for configuring and testing the lifecycle decisions discussed in the book.

https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/liveness-readiness-startup-probes/

https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/

Cache expiration and eviction: Chapter 5.

Redis documents expiration and memory-driven eviction separately. Both affect cache misses, but they settle different configuration decisions.

https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/expire/

https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/

Replication and admission-state durability: Chapter 14.

Redis’s replication documentation and WAIT reference explain why replication acknowledgments alone cannot promise a lossless, strongly consistent admission counter across failover.

https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/replication/

https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/wait/

Log processing and delivery guarantees: Chapter 12.

Apache Kafka’s design guide covers partitions, consumers, replication, and delivery semantics. Its transactional guarantees do not automatically include an external database or payment provider. The link below is to the Kafka 4.0 documentation; use the documentation for your cluster version.

https://kafka.apache.org/40/design/design/

Stateful stream recovery: Chapter 12.

Apache Flink describes checkpoints and the recovery of application state. Its treatment of external sinks is useful when evaluating end-to-end delivery claims.

https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/learn-flink/fault_tolerance/

Coordination failures: Chapter 14.

The etcd failure guide describes leader failure, quorum loss, and network partitions. Its examples help assess a regional ownership service and the conditions under which it must refuse a transfer.

https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/op-guide/failures/

Training and serving consistency: Chapter 13.

Google’s Rules of Machine Learning includes guidance on training-serving skew, feature validation, and testing the infrastructure around a model.

https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml

Inference measurements: Chapter 13.

vLLM’s production metrics reference includes queue time, active and waiting requests, KV-cache usage, token counts, and inference latency. Metric names and measurement boundaries depend on the deployed runtime version.

https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/usage/metrics/

HTTP caching: Appendix B.

RFC 9111 specifies cache behavior and response directives, including no-store. These matter when short links need bounded revocation.

https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html

Authorization review: Appendix C.

OWASP’s Authorization Cheat Sheet covers least privilege, resource-level checks, denial by default, and negative tests across trust boundaries.

https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html

Capacity and Performance

John Allspaw, The Art of Capacity Planning. An operational treatment of measuring, forecasting, and planning capacity. It complements the workload calculations in Chapters 1 and 2.

Connie U. Smith and Lloyd G. Williams, Performance Solutions: A Practical Guide to Creating Responsive, Scalable Software. Develops performance modeling as part of software design, including the relationship between workload assumptions and architectural choices.

Leonard Kleinrock, Queueing Systems, Volume 1: Theory. A mathematical treatment for readers who want to study queueing models and their assumptions beyond the estimates used in this book.

Distributed State and Data Systems

Martin Kleppmann and Chris Riccomini, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, second edition. Provides a broader treatment of storage, replication, transactions, distributed coordination, and data processing. It is especially useful alongside Chapters 3, 7, 11, 12, and 14.

Roberto Vitillo, Understanding Distributed Systems, second edition. Connects networking, consistency, scalability, and reliability. It offers additional background for readers encountering distributed systems concepts for the first time.

Kyle Kingsbury, An Introduction to Distributed Systems. An online course with readings and exercises covering system models, consistency, and coordination.

https://github.com/aphyr/distsys-class

Production Reliability

Michael T. Nygard, Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software, second edition. Examines production failure mechanisms and stability patterns, including timeouts, circuit breakers, and bulkheads. It is a useful companion to Chapters 4 and 9.

Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, and Niall Richard Murphy, editors, Site Reliability Engineering. Describes reliability practices including service objectives, monitoring, capacity planning, and incident response.

Betsy Beyer, Niall Richard Murphy, David K. Rensin, Kent Kawahara, and Stephen Thorne, editors, The Site Reliability Workbook. Develops practical applications of SRE methods through worked examples and case studies.

Both Google SRE books are available online:

https://sre.google/books/

Observability

Charity Majors, Liz Fong-Jones, and George Miranda, Observability Engineering. Explores instrumentation, investigative workflows, and the use of detailed events to understand production behavior. It extends the measurement and diagnosis work in Chapter 8.

Deployment and Delivery

Jez Humble and David Farley, Continuous Delivery: Reliable Software Releases through Build, Test, and Deployment Automation. Covers deployment pipelines, testing, configuration, and release practices relevant to Chapters 6 and 10.

Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble, and Gene Kim, Accelerate: The Science of Lean Software and DevOps. Examines research on software delivery performance and organizational capabilities, alongside the limits of individual delivery metrics.

Marko Lukša and Kevin Conner, Kubernetes in Action, second edition. Explains Kubernetes workloads, networking, configuration, and lifecycle management. Consult the documentation for your deployed Kubernetes version before applying configuration examples.

Service Boundaries

Sam Newman, Building Microservices, second edition. Examines service boundaries, communication, data ownership, and the operating requirements introduced by decomposition.

Sam Newman, Monolith to Microservices. Concentrates on incremental migration and the choices involved in extracting services from an existing application.

Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software. Develops the domain modeling and bounded-context concepts used in Chapter 11.

Event Processing

Gwen Shapira, Todd Palino, Rajini Sivaram, and Krit Petty, Kafka: The Definitive Guide, second edition. Provides implementation detail on producers, consumers, replication, delivery guarantees, and Kafka operations.

Ben Stopford, Designing Event-Driven Systems. Examines event-streaming applications and the relationship between events, state, and service integration.

Machine Learning and AI Applications

Chip Huyen, Designing Machine Learning Systems. Covers data preparation, features, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring across the production machine-learning lifecycle.

Chip Huyen, AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models. Extends the discussion to applications built with pretrained models, including evaluation, retrieval, inference, and application design.

Emmanuel Ameisen, Building Machine Learning Powered Applications. Follows the work required to turn a model-based idea into an application, including dataset construction and evaluation.

Research and Case Studies

Adrian Colyer’s The Morning Paper contains accessible discussions of research papers, including distributed systems and data processing. The archive can lead readers to the original papers behind an implementation technique.

https://blog.acolyer.org/

Jepsen publishes investigations of distributed-system behavior under faults. These reports are useful examples of connecting a claimed guarantee to a test and interpreting the resulting history.

https://jepsen.io/analyses

Sources for the Public Postmortems

The case-study boxes in the chapters summarize published incidents. The original reports provide their timelines, technical evidence, and details omitted from the shorter discussions. The Knight Capital account is an SEC administrative order rather than an engineering postmortem.

Cache repair overload: Chapter 5.

Facebook Engineering, “More Details on Today’s Outage,” September 2010. https://engineering.fb.com/2010/09/23/uncategorized/more-details-on-today-s-outage/

Failover and divergent writes: Chapter 7.

GitHub Engineering, “October 21 post-incident analysis,” October 2018. https://github.blog/news-insights/company-news/oct21-post-incident-analysis/

Recovery tooling that shares fate: Chapter 8.

Santosh Janardhan, “More details about the October 4 outage,” Meta Engineering, October 2021. https://engineering.fb.com/2021/10/05/networking-traffic/outage-details/

Operator input and capacity floors: Chapter 9.

Amazon Web Services, “Summary of the Amazon S3 Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region,” March 2017. https://aws.amazon.com/message/41926/

Partial deployment and reused flags: Chapter 10.

U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, In the Matter of Knight Capital Americas LLC, Exchange Act Release No. 70694, October 2013. https://www.sec.gov/litigation/admin/2013/34-70694.pdf

Configuration that executes: Chapter 10.

John Graham-Cumming, “Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019,” Cloudflare Blog, July 2019. https://blog.cloudflare.com/details-of-the-cloudflare-outage-on-july-2-2019/
